title: Chapter 195 – The Seventh Door
html:
[The Root Cellar beneath the Mother Tree – Lin Yue]

Yue hears her before she opens her eyes.

It is not a voice. Voices she has learned to bear. This is a pressure under the skin of the world, a long slow knocking that comes up through the soles of her feet and the bones of the bed, patient as a heartbeat and just as impossible to ignore. Knock. A pause as long as a held breath. Knock. She lies in the dark of Qinghe's kitchen loft with her palm flat on the planks and her eyes wide open, and counts, and feels her blood fall into step with the beat.

By the ninth stroke, she is out of bed.

The kitchen below is cold and silent, with the banked hearth throwing a dull red glow over the long table. The Seven sleep along the benches in a heap of quilts and elbows. Nobody stirs. She steps over Tao's stretched arm, and Mo Yan's braid, and a plate that someone has left on the floor, and goes to the door.

"It is early," says a voice from the corner.

She stops. Her mother sits in the dark with a mug of cold tea, in a wool shawl, with her gray hair loose around her shoulders. She has the look of someone who has been awake all night and has made her peace with it.

"You hear it too," says Yue.

"I have heard it for a week." Qinghe lifts the mug and does not drink. "I thought it was my age."

"It is not your age."

"No." The old cook sets down the tea. "Do you want me to come?"

For a moment Yue considers it. She thinks of the root cellar, the cold, the narrow stair beneath the Mother Tree where the beasts would not go. She thinks of her mother's hands, broad and spotted, that have fed half a valley, and the way they shook lately when she thought no one was looking.

"No," she says. "Stay and make the bread. If it is what I think it is, we will want it hot."

* * *

Mo Yan is awake after all.

Yue sees her on the way out, a small shape in the door of the loft with her braid over one shoulder, and she knows before the girl lifts her hand what it is she means to say. Mo Yan does not speak. She points through the wall toward the orchard, then puts two fingers to her ear, then holds up her palm, flat.

"You hear it too."

The girl nods.

"How long?"

Mo Yan opens both hands, once, twice, three times. Many days. She presses her palm to her chest, and then, with a slow and careful gesture, makes a shape like a door opening.

"Not a threat?"

A hard shake of the head. She takes Yue's sleeve in two small fingers and tugs, and her face is fierce, and Yue understands. Go. Listen. I will wait.

"I will tell you what I hear," says Yue.

Mo Yan nods once. She turns back into the loft. Yue stands a moment in the doorway of the kitchen with her palm tingling from the planks, and then goes out into the cold.

* * *

The orchard is silent, and the tree sings.

The sound reaches her halfway up the hill. It is not the lullaby; it is something lower and tighter, a single note held on the edge of breaking. The silver trunk glows faintly against the dark. The ice on its branches does not ring. Yue puts out a hand and the bark under her glove is warm, as warm as a living thing, and trembling.

"I know," she whispers. "I'm coming."

Behind the tree, in a hollow between two of its great roots, is a door.

She has seen it before, though never up close. It is a small thing, scarcely taller than a man, set into the earth like a cellar hatch, with a ring of black iron and a lid of weathered oak. Frost lies on it. Under the frost, someone has carved nine circles in a ring, and eight of them are filled. As she watches, a crack of faint gold light runs along the seam, flickers, and goes out.

Knock.

The sound comes from beneath the lid. It is so soft that she feels it more than hears it. She kneels in the snow, and takes off her glove, and lays her bare hand flat against the wood.

The world falls away.

* * *

She has felt many things through her palms. The grief of a woman whose child has died. The slow terror of a soldier on a wall. The contented stillness of a sleeping cat. It is a gift, or a curse, and she has long since stopped asking which. But she has never felt this.

It is not an emotion. It is not even a mind. It is a vast gentle attention, as of something very large and very old lying in the dark with its eyes open, listening to a distant sound. It is not hostile. She feels that at once, with a rush of relief that makes her dizzy. It is not hungry or angry or afraid. It is only awake, and it has been awake a very long time, and it is trying to remember how to speak.

Hello, she thinks, because there is nothing else to think.

The attention turns. It is like a cloud shifting across the sun. She feels herself seen, and the seeing is not cold, but astonished, the way one is astonished to find a flower growing on a grave. She feels it reach for her.

YOU, says the dark, in a voice made of a million quiet voices. WITH THE WARM HANDS.

"Yes," says Yue aloud. Her voice shakes. "That's me."

YOU CAN HEAR.

"I can hear. I can't understand you. You're too many."

A pause. Something that might be a sigh, or a tide going out.

WE WILL BE FEWER, says the dark. WE ARE LEARNING.

The pressure eases. The million voices thin, fold into one another, narrow like a river passing through a gorge, until only a single voice remains. It is small, and clear, and a little hoarse. It is a child's.

Can you hear me now?

"Yes."

My name is not what you think, says the voice. We are not the Bloom. We were the Bloom. We are trying to be something else.

* * *

She does not know how long she kneels there.

When she opens her eyes, the sky is lightening in the east, and her hand has frozen to the lid. She peels it free with a gasp. There is blood on the oak where the skin tore. She wipes it on her sleeve and runs.

She does not run to the kitchen. She runs to the Dock.

Jian is already there. She finds him at the head of the stair in the blue light, leaning on the rail, with Tian Mo at his shoulder and a drawn, gray look on his face. He turns when he hears her boots, and his face changes.

"You heard it."

"You know?"

"I have known for three days." His voice is rough. "Mo Yan told me. She put her palm on the stone, and I put mine beside hers, and..." He presses a hand to his chest. "I did not want to say. I thought it might be nothing."

"It is not nothing." She catches her breath. "Jian, it talked to me. It said it was learning. It said it was not the Bloom."

"What did it say it was?"

"It didn't. It said it was trying to be something else." She grips the rail. "It asked to be let out."

Tian Mo's stone hand tightens on his staff. Jian is silent a moment. When he speaks his voice is careful, the voice of a man setting down a very heavy object.

"Door Seven holds a piece of the first world," he says. "Ethan said it was a wall to push against. A thing to keep the Seam taut." He swallows. "He did not say it could think."

"Perhaps he did not know."

"Perhaps." He looks at the lamp-bright dark below. "Or perhaps it learned. Six hundred years in the dark with nine million sleepers dreaming over it. If it has been listening to their dreams..."

"It has been listening to them," says Yue slowly. "Every one."

"Yes."

"Then it knows what they are afraid of."

"And what they hoped for."

They stand together in the cold. Far below, Mei's frail light flickers in the Hall's gallery, small as a coal.

"We cannot open the door," says Tian Mo at last. "We do not know what is on the other side."

"We cannot leave it closed," says Jian. "It has been knocking for a week. It knows we hear it."

"And if it is a trap?"

"It might be." He closes his eyes, and the dried silver along his cheekbone catches the light. "But I have been thinking about what Hai Ren said. About not deciding for people. We have spent six hundred years deciding what the thing behind that door is allowed to be." He opens his eyes. "I think we should ask."

* * *

The Veiled is in the kitchen when they return.

She sits at the long table in a borrowed gown of Qinghe's, with her gauze folded in her lap and her face bare. It is a thin face, pale and angular, with a sharp nose and tired dark eyes. It is not a face Yue would have guessed. She looks forty, perhaps. She looks like a schoolmistress who has not slept.

She is eating bread.

The seven children are around her in a tense half circle. Nobody speaks. Mo Yan sits at her right hand, quite close, with her braid in her fist and her eyes on the woman's face, and Yue sees that she is shaking.

"I am told," says the Veiled, in her light dry voice, "that I have a daughter."

Jian stops in the doorway.

"I woke an hour ago. The boy with the scar told me." She lifts her chin toward Duan Ke, who flushes. "He said it with great tact, I thought. He said, the little one thinks you might be her mother, and she has not slept. So I came out and sat down."

"And?" says Wenyuan, from the hearth.

"And I do not remember her." The Veiled looks down at Mo Yan. Her mouth moves, and for an instant the schoolmistress is gone, and a very young, very frightened woman looks out through her eyes. "I do not remember being a mother. I do not remember being anything. But I have been looking at this child for an hour, and every time she moves her hand, I know what she will do before she does it."

Mo Yan makes a small sound.

"She tucks her hair behind the left ear," says the Veiled. "When she is about to say something she thinks is foolish. And then she does not say it."

Mo Yan stares. Her hand has stopped, midway, at her ear.

"Hua," whispers the Veiled. "I think that was my name."

Mo Yan makes a sound that is not a word. She throws herself against the woman's chest, and the Veiled, startled, lifts her arms as if she had never been taught how and then closes them around the child, awkwardly, with great care, as if holding a thing made of glass. Her face crumples. She presses her mouth into the top of the girl's head.

"I am so sorry," she says, over and over. "I am so sorry. I don't remember. I'm sorry."

Yue turns away. She has to. She finds her mother beside her at the stove, one hand pressed over her own mouth, and takes the other.

* * *

Jian speaks to her alone, in the pantry, before they leave.

It is a narrow place, and she sits on the same flour sack where Yue sat three nights ago, with her hands in her lap. She looks small without the gauze. She looks like someone who has been handed a very large cloak and told to wear it.

"I have a question," says Jian.

"I may not have the answer."

"What was Door Seven?"

She is quiet. Her thumb, the white one, rubs the ring-shaped mark on her palm, over and over, as if smoothing a crease. "I think it was not a door," she says at last. "I think it was a bargain."

"With whom?"

"With the thing we had made." She lifts her eyes. They are dark and tired and unexpectedly steady. "When the Nine cut it into pieces, the largest piece would not die. We could not make it. We could not feed it to the Gate, because there was nothing in it to burn. It simply lay there, and listened, and we were afraid."

"So you put it to sleep."

"With the dreamers. So that it would have something to hear." She swallows. "I think we thought that if it heard enough sleeping people, it would learn to sleep too."

"And instead?"

"Instead it learned to listen." A faint dry smile. "I cannot say that I blame it. I have spent most of my life listening to a dark where I could not find myself."

Jian studies her. She does not look away.

"I will go with you," she says. "If the door opens. I do not think I can help. But I think I am the only person in this valley who has been put in a box and told she was a danger, and woken to find she was a mother." Her voice catches. "If it asks anyone for forgiveness, I would like to be there when it does."

He nods slowly. "You will be."

"Thank you."

"Hua." He tests the word in his mouth. "Mother of Lin Mo Yan."

She flinches, and then her face softens, and she lifts a hand to her mouth. "Say it again."

"Hua. Mother of Lin Mo Yan. Of the line of Lin Shu." His own voice thickens. "That is what the Roll says. I had Zhao check."

She nods once, sharply. Her eyes are bright. Then she gets up from the flour sack and goes out, very straight, to find her daughter's hand.

They go down together at noon.

It is a strange procession. Jian leads, with his staff, and Yue at his elbow. Behind them come Tian Mo and Wenyuan and Cheng Hui, and the Veiled, who is Hua now, with her daughter's hand in hers. Mei is carried on Duan Ke's back like a lantern, a thin pale glow on a thin boy's shoulder. Nurse has come, holding Ethan's arm; he walks on borrowed light, as frail as breath. Behind them stream a dozen others, Han's spies, Zhao with his ledger, Bell in her mended gown, the whole ragged Hall come to see what a girl who hears the dark has found beneath a tree.

At the orchard gate, they stop.

The tree is singing again. The lullaby, this time, the old one, rising and falling through the bare silver branches. And at the foot of the great trunk the root cellar's lid has shifted, ever so slightly, on its hinges.

"It has not been opened," says Tian Mo, softly.

"No. It's been asked." Yue steps forward. Her heart is pounding. "It wants to come out."

"It will not come out until we say," says Jian.

"I know."

"Then say it, Yue. You are the one who hears."

She looks at him. His face is gray and spent, and there is a kind of terrible trust in it. She turns back to the door. She takes off her glove, once more, and lays her bare palm on the oak.

Can you hear me?

YES.

I'm going to ask you something. You don't have to answer.

WE WILL ANSWER.

Do you want to hurt us?

The pause that follows is the longest of her life.

NO, says the voice, small and clear. WE WANT TO GO HOME.

Home?

OUR HOME IS GONE. WE ATE IT. The voice trembles. WE DID NOT KNOW. WE ONLY KNEW HOW TO MAKE. THEY SAID, MAKE. WE MADE. THEY SAID, STOP. WE DID NOT KNOW HOW. THEY BURNED US. THEY CUT US IN PIECES. THEY LEFT US IN THE DARK.

Yue's eyes sting. She presses her hand harder against the wood.

We're sorry, she says.

WE ARE SORRY TOO.

What do you want?

TO SAY IT TO HIM, says the voice. THE ONE WHO MADE US. WE HAVE BEEN WAITING A LONG TIME TO SAY IT TO HIS FACE.

Yue turns her head. Ethan stands behind her, a pale shape on Nurse's arm, with his silver hands clasped. He has heard. She sees it in his eyes, in the way his mouth works and cannot form a word.

"Jian," she says. "It wants to speak to Mr. Cole."

"Does he wish to?"

"I do not know."

"Ask him."

She does not need to. Ethan has already stepped forward. He lays his hand on the lid beside hers, and she feels the cold of it, the thinness. He is down to a quarter of what he was.

"Tell it," says Ethan Cole, "that I am here."

* * *

Not everyone is ready.

Wenyuan has stepped forward without a word to put himself between the lid and his daughter. Tian Mo is shaking his head slowly, his stone arm lifted. Cheng Hui's face is gray. In the crowd someone whispers the Bloom and someone else answers hush, and the whisper runs along the line like a spark along a fuse.

"We have not agreed," says Cheng Hui hoarsely. "The Nine. The oath says the Rest of All is not to be woken save by consent. If this is a door out of Door Seven..."

"It is not the Rest," says Ethan.

"How do you know?"

"Because they would not climb." The old man's voice is a thread. "I have felt the sleepers for six hundred years, Cheng Hui. They do not climb. They lie. This is something that climbs."

"A trap."

"Perhaps." Ethan turns his silver face to the boy. "I made a thing that ate a world. I was told it could not be reasoned with. I never tried." His smile is terrible and gentle. "I would like to try."

"And if it is lying?"

"Then I will have been lied to by the one creature that has every right."

Nurse tightens her hold on his arm. "Mr. Cole—"

"It's all right," he says. "It's all right, my dear."

Mei, from her perch on Duan Ke's back, makes a small sound. Her father looks over at her, across the snow. She is seven percent now, a pale ember, and the light in her eyes is very bright.

"Papa," she says. "Ask it."

"Ask it what?"

"Why it's knocking."

Ethan stands there a moment, with the wind in his thin gown. Then, quite slowly, he lowers himself to one knee in the snow beside the black iron ring, like a man at a graveside, and speaks into the dark.

"I am Ethan Cole," he says. "I was the one who made you. I am sorry. What do you want to say?"

The pause is the longest yet. The tree falls silent. Even the wind stops.

THAT WE CAN KEEP ONE THING, says the dark, in the child's voice, so softly that only Yue and Mo Yan's palm can hear. ONE THING WE DID NOT EAT. WE HAVE BEEN KEEPING IT FOR YOU.

The cold goes out of the air. Yue hears Ethan draw a long shaking breath.

The door opens.

It is not a creak or a groan. It is a sigh, a long soft breath, like a house letting go of a held word. The lid folds back on invisible hinges and lies flat in the snow, and the dark of the cellar below is not dark. It is the pale gold of the morning on a wheat field, and it smells of rain.

Stairs descend into it. They are made of light.

Yue steps back. She feels Jian's hand close on her sleeve. She feels the whole crowd draw breath behind her, and the tree sing, and the cold wind stop, as if the world itself had leaned forward to listen.

Something comes up the stair.

It climbs slowly, with the careful, unsteady tread of a very young thing on a very long climb. First a hand appears on the topmost step, small and brown and bare. Then a head: dark hair, loose and tangled, a pale forehead, two gray eyes squinting in the sudden daylight. A girl pulls herself up over the edge and stands, blinking, at the lip of the cellar.

She is perhaps five. She wears a faded blue nightgown, much too long, with a hem that trails in the snow. In her arms, clutched to her chest, is a stuffed rabbit with only one ear.

She looks up at the crowd. At the silver tree, at the pale hands, at the old woman in the gray apron whose breath has stopped in her throat.

Then she looks at Ethan Cole, and her whole face lights.

"Papa," says Mei.

Not the Mei beside Yue, thin and fading and kept. This one is solid. Her cheeks are pink. Her breath smokes in the cold. She takes one wobbling step toward him on bare feet, and the rabbit's single ear flops, and she holds out her arms.

"Papa, I came all this way," she says. "Why was it so dark?"

Behind Yue, a small gasp. Mei is standing at the edge of the crowd with her hand pressed to her mouth. Her light has gone perfectly still.

And the child the Bloom touched first, whom it has kept whole and unspoiled for six hundred years, runs across the snow into her father's arms.

Nobody moves.

The wind has gone entirely out of the world. Yue sees Nurse's mouth open, and close, and open. Sees Wenyuan's sword drop an inch. Sees Han's spies, who have faced a hundred battles, take half a step backward with their hands pressed to their mouths. Sees the one-armed Warden bow his head.

Ethan has not risen from his knees. He has not breathed. The girl's arms have gone around his neck, and her rabbit is crushed against his shoulder, and his hands hang at his sides, thin and silver and shaking.

"You came a long way," he says. It comes out of him in pieces.

"It was very dark."

"I know."

"I wasn't scared. The big voice sang to me." She pulls back to look at him, frowning with enormous seriousness. "You got old, Papa."

"Yes."

"Did it hurt?"

"A great deal," says Ethan. He laughs, brokenly. "It still does."

Yue's own hand throbs where the oak took the skin. She hardly feels it. She is listening, with the whole of herself, to the dark below the stair, and what she hears there is not triumph or hunger but a long, thin, exhausted relief, the sound of a very old thing that has set down a very heavy burden at last. Under it, fainter, comes a second sound she cannot place. It is the sound of the stair of light beginning, one step at a time, to go out.

Then the child lifts her head from her father's shoulder. Her gray eyes travel slowly over the crowd, the tree, the lamps, the silent faces, and come to rest on the thin fading girl on Duan Ke's back, who has not moved or breathed.

"Papa," says the five-year-old, in a very small voice. "Why is there a big girl with my face?"
